agent_notes: The Hebrew numbers the superscription as verse 1 (and verse 2 as the historical note); the KJV leaves both unnumbered (52:0) and begins at 52:1 with Hebrew verse 3. Every KJV number in this psalm is therefore Hebrew minus 2.

lamnatzeach is glossed 'to the choirmaster' following the STEPBible gloss and the tradition of the chief musician; the exact duty of the office (leader, director, 'for the overseer', as YLT) is uncertain. maskil is left transliterated in the gloss, with 'skilful poem / instruction' as a probable sense; the Targum reads 'good insight'.

ki asita ('for you have done') has no stated object; I leave it open in the literal layer and in the dramatic one, though Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri take it to mean the judgment on Doeg. Meiri notes the perfect stands for a future. 'it is good' in the last colon: the subject of tov is shimkha, 'your name' (so ASV, KJV), not the praise; BBE reads otherwise.

agent_notes: Revised per the reviewer: the added line 'You, who think the day is yours' is removed from the dramatic layer, so 'every hour of the day' belongs only to God's faithful love. agent_notes: 'oseh remiyyah is ambiguous: it can describe the razor (YLT, ASV, KJV, 'working deceit') or address Doeg (vocative). I chose the vocative 'O doer of deceit' because the participle is masculine and the STEPBible gloss reads it so; lashon is common gender, so this is a judgment call. The packet's Targum and Radak/Meiri treat the razor as the deceitful one.

agent_notes: ma'uzzo (Radak notes its doubled zayin) comes from the same root as ya'oz, 'be strong', so 'refuge' and 'took strength' form a wordplay I keep. behavvato is the same noun hawwah as in verse 4; the KJV's 'wickedness' here and 'mischiefs' there hides that the psalmist repeats a word.
